findings.summary: American Wire Gauge (AWG) is a North American logarithmic stepped standard for electrically conducting round wire diameters, defined by ASTM B258 since 1857. It assigns smaller numbers to thicker wires; each successive gauge represents a constant diameter ratio of the 39th root of 92. The system originated from wire drawing operations and differs from metric standards by specifying diameter rather than cross-sectional area. AWG tables provide diameter, area, resistance, and ampacity data for solid copper conductors, with stranded wire area calculated to an equivalent solid conductor.

mechanisms.title: Diameter progression
mechanisms.explanation: Each AWG gauge step changes diameter by a constant geometric ratio. The ratio between any two successive gauges is the 39th root of 92 (approximately 1.124), meaning diameters decrease logarithmically as gauge numbers increase. Larger gauges (smaller numbers) are produced through more drawing operations.

mechanisms.title: Area and conductance rules of thumb
mechanisms.explanation: Cross-sectional area approximately doubles for every 3-gauge decrease, and diameter doubles for every 6-gauge decrease. A 10-gauge decrease multiplies area, weight, and conductance by approximately 10. Copper resistance is roughly 1 ohm per 1000 feet at 10 AWG, scaling by a factor of 10 per 10-gauge step.

unknowns: Exact physical drawing process details for historical gauge standardization

Precise manufacturing tolerances for very fine wires below 30 AWG
